qs.q: A patient with a high tibial fracture presents with loss of dorsiflexion and foot drop. Which anatomical structure is most likely compromised?
o: The common peroneal nerve wrapping around the fibular neck
The tibial nerve running deep within the popliteal fossa
The sciatic nerve bifurcating within the gluteal region
The femoral nerve passing inferior to the inguinal ligament
The obturator nerve traveling through the obturator foramen
qs.e: The common peroneal nerve is superficial at the fibular neck, making it vulnerable to high tibial fractures.

ai.title: Foot Drop
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Foot drop is weakness of ankle dorsiflexion caused by peripheral nerve or root lesions. Recognise the pattern, identify common tropical causes, and organise focused investigations and early management.

b: Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion (≤3/5) with preserved plantarflexion
Inability to lift the foot during swing phase (steppage gait)
Positive heel‑walk test confirms dorsiflexor weakness
sections.p: Foot drop describes loss of active ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, producing a high‑stepping gait. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by weakness of tibialis anterior (MRC ≤3) and a positive “heel‑walk” test.

b: MRC 5‑4: mild, may walk unaided
MRC 3‑2: requires ankle‑foot orthosis (AFO) or cane
MRC ≤1: severe, risk of falls, needs assistive device
sections.p: Severity is graded by the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale for muscle power and by functional impact on gait.

b: Common fibular (peroneal) nerve compression at the fibular head – prolonged squatting, leg crossing, tight casts
L5 radiculopathy – lumbar disc prolapse, spondylolisthesis
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy – especially with poor glycaemic control
HIV‑associated neuropathy – antiretroviral toxic neuropathy or opportunistic infection
Tuberculous meningitis or spinal TB – compressive radiculopathy
Malaria‑related neuropathy – rare but reported after severe falciparum infection
Traumatic fibular fracture or knee dislocation
sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings, the most frequent aetiologies are peripheral nerve compression, infectious neuropathies and trauma.

b: Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and eversion
Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg (if nerve lesion)
Steppage gait to avoid toe‑dragging
Possible foot ulceration from abnormal pressure
sections.p: Patients notice difficulty lifting the front of the foot, tripping, and a characteristic high‑stepping gait. Sensory loss may accompany the motor deficit if the nerve is affected.

t.b: Confirms site and extent of motor/sensory loss; guides localisation

t.a: Straight‑leg raise and lumbar spine exam
t.b: Distinguishes radicular from peripheral nerve cause
Identifies demyelinating vs axonal injury and localises lesion; if unavailable, rely on clinical localisation
Detects compressive lesions or cysts; if not available, use careful palpation for tenderness
Shows disc herniation or TB spondylitis; if MRI unavailable, consider plain X‑ray for vertebral collapse and refer
Screens for diabetic neuropathy; treat hyperglycaemia if elevated
Detects HIV‑related neuropathy; start ART optimisation if positive
Look for infection or inflammatory causes; elevated ESR/CRP may suggest TB or pyogenic infection

b: Rapidly progressive weakness, bilateral involvement
Severe back pain with fever – possible spinal epidural abscess
Foot ulcer or gangrene – risk of infection
Signs of systemic infection (fever, weight loss) – consider TB or HIV
sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent referral or admission.

b: Remove compressive factors – adjust casts, advise against prolonged leg crossing, physiotherapy for stretching
If L5 radiculopathy from disc – trial NSAID (e.g., ibuprofen) and physiotherapy; avoid steroids if active infection suspected
Diabetic neuropathy – optimise glycaemic control, prescribe gabapentin for neuropathic pain if needed
HIV neuropathy – review ART regimen, switch neurotoxic drugs (e.g., stavudine) if present
TB spine – refer for anti‑TB therapy and possible surgical decompression
AFO (ankle‑foot orthosis) for functional support
Physiotherapy: dorsiflexion strengthening, gait training, balance exercises
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive measures to preserve function and prevent complications.

b: Re‑assess muscle power every 4‑6 weeks
Monitor blood glucose and HIV parameters
Educate on proper footwear and foot hygiene to avoid ulcers
Encourage early mobilisation with orthosis
sections.p: Regular review ensures recovery, detects complications and reinforces preventive measures.

b: Drop foot due to peripheral nerve vs. foot inversion weakness from tibial nerve palsy
Cerebellar ataxic gait – unsteady, not high‑stepping
Charcot‑Marie‑Tooth disease – chronic distal weakness, not acute
sections.p: Conditions that mimic foot drop must be distinguished.

b: Normal EMG early in compressive neuropathy – repeat after 2‑3 weeks if suspicion remains
Normal MRI lumbar spine does not exclude radiculopathy from inflammatory causes; consider contrast or CT myelography
sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.

whenToSeekHelp: Associated fever, back pain or urinary retention
Development of foot ulcer or gangrene
